Chapter 5: The Power of Financial Education—Why Schools Don’t Teach Money Skills
Isn’t it interesting how we spend years in school learning algebra, history, and science, but barely touch on the topic of money? Most of us leave the classroom able to solve for X, but when it comes to creating a budget, investing in stocks, or starting a business, we’re left in the dark.
This is a gap that catches a lot of people off guard as they step into adulthood. The story of the boy really brings this to life. His own father was highly educated—he had the degrees, the knowledge, and the steady job. But when it came to handling money, he struggled. He knew how to earn a paycheck, but not how to make his money grow or work for him.
On the other hand, the friend’s father—who didn’t have as much formal education—seemed to have cracked the code on building wealth. It’s a contrast that makes you wonder, why don’t schools teach us about money? Well, a lot of it comes down to tradition. Our education system was built for a time when lifelong jobs and pensions were the norm. But times have changed. Job security isn’t what it used to be. If you rely only on a paycheck, you might find yourself vulnerable—facing layoffs, economic shifts, or those surprise expenses that seem to come out of nowhere.
The friend’s father believed that understanding how money works is the most important skill anyone can learn. He pushed the boys to read books, attend seminars, and seek out mentors. He’d remind them that financial education isn’t something you pick up once and forget. It’s ongoing. The world of money keeps changing, and if you stop learning, you can quickly fall behind.
But here’s something to pay attention to: knowledge alone isn’t enough. It’s easy to read about investing or entrepreneurship, but real understanding comes from rolling up your sleeves and getting in the game—buying that first stock, starting a side business, or negotiating your first deal. Sure, you’ll make mistakes. But each one is a lesson you just can’t find in a textbook.
Over time, the boy realized that financial education goes way beyond numbers. It’s about your mindset, your habits, and your willingness to keep learning, no matter what. When you take charge of your own education, opportunities start to show up where others only see roadblocks. You become more resilient, more adaptable, and you build a life that isn’t limited by fear—or by what everyone else thinks is possible.
